VISIT NOTE (draft)

**Patient:** Sophia
**Visit type:** Follow-up for right knee injury and diabetes management

**Chief complaint:** Right knee injury.

**HPI:** Patient reports slipping while jumping on a trampoline about four days ago, landing on the right knee. She felt a pop at the time, followed by significant swelling. She took ibuprofen and applied ice with partial relief. She can bear weight but reports pain with standing and considerable difficulty getting around. Pain is localized to the inside of the knee (patient describes the inner part of the kneecap).

**Diabetes:** Patient reports her diabetes is "going okay." She acknowledges she often forgets to check her blood sugar. Reports her diet has been "pretty good."

**Physical exam:**
- Cardiac: Heart sounds normal, no murmurs or gallops.
- Respiratory: Lungs clear.
- Right knee: Visible swelling. Tenderness to palpation on the medial side, with less pain laterally. Pain with knee flexion and extension, with mildly limited range of motion. McMurray test negative.

**Assessment:**
1. Right knee injury. Clinician is concerned for an MCL (medial collateral ligament) tear or injury, given the reported pop, weight-bearing difficulty, and medial tenderness.
2. Type 2 diabetes, being treated by primary care. Clinician notes she is managing it reasonably well. (Diabetes type not stated in transcript; verify.)

**Plan:**
1. Right knee:
   - Straight-leg brace.
   - Mobic prescribed for pain and swelling.
   - Ice the knee for about 15 minutes, once an hour.
   - MRI of the right knee to evaluate the suspected MCL injury and check for other damage.
2. Diabetes:
   - Recheck hemoglobin A1c.
   - Refill metformin 500 mg; continue current dose.

**Patient education/disposition:** Patient agreed with the plan and had no further questions.

VISIT NOTE (draft)

**Chief complaint:** Difficulty urinating.

**HPI:** Patient reports about 6 months of urinary symptoms, possibly longer, that have gradually worsened. He describes a weak urinary stream and incomplete emptying, sometimes needing to stand and wait to void more. He wakes up 3 to 4 times a night to urinate despite emptying his bladder before bed and limiting evening fluids. He denies burning on urination. He had one episode of diarrhea last week, which he attributes to something he ate. He denies any history of urinary retention requiring catheterization. He has not previously seen a urologist.

**Cardiac:** History of coronary artery disease with a stent placed in the right coronary artery (around 2018). Patient saw cardiologist Dr. Moore in November and was told everything was okay. He reports he is still performing his daily activities and is "kind of" exercising. Chest pain and shortness of breath were not clearly addressed in the transcript.

**Diabetes:** Patient reports he is trying to follow his diet and believes his blood sugars are okay. He is taking metformin.

**Exam:**
- Heart: Slight 3/6 systolic ejection murmur, heard best at the left base.
- Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
- Abdomen: Nontender, nondistended. No masses, rebound, or guarding.
- Prostate (rectal exam): Enlarged. No masses.

**Assessment and plan:**

1. **Lower urinary tract symptoms / difficulty urinating, with enlarged prostate on exam**
   - Routine labs, PSA, urinalysis, and urine culture ordered.
   - Start Flomax (tamsulosin) 0.4 mg once daily, taken at night due to risk of dizziness.
   - Referral to urology. Physician to contact urology directly and request an appointment this week.
   - Patient asked about an over-the-counter prostate supplement seen in a commercial. Physician stated he was not familiar with its effectiveness and recommended Flomax with urology follow-up.

2. **Coronary artery disease, s/p RCA stent; systolic murmur**
   - Echocardiogram ordered to follow up the murmur.
   - Continue Lipitor 40 mg daily, aspirin, and metoprolol.
   - Lipid panel ordered.

3. **Type 2 diabetes** *(diagnosis type not stated in transcript; confirm)*
   - Continue metformin 1000 mg twice daily.
   - Hemoglobin A1c ordered to guide any adjustments.

**Follow-up:** Return in 3 to 4 weeks. Patient instructed to call or message through the patient portal with any concerns. Patient verbalized understanding and had no questions about the lab orders.

VISIT NOTE (draft)

**Patient:** Louis, 58-year-old male
**Visit type:** Follow-up from emergency room visit

**Chief complaint:** Shortness of breath after playing tennis; follow-up from ER visit.

**History of present illness:**
Patient played tennis on Saturday in hot, humid conditions. After about 30 minutes, he became very short of breath and had difficulty breathing. He thought he was having a heart attack and was very anxious. His wife took him to the ER, where he reports that "everything checked out." Approximately six hours after arriving home, he felt lightheaded and dizzy. He felt fine on Sunday. He has been taking his heart failure medications as prescribed and reports good adherence. He is in contact with his cardiologist/physician. He reports occasional dietary sodium indiscretion ("cheats every now and then") but otherwise avoids salty and junk foods.

**Interval history:**
- Cataract removal about three months ago. No vision problems since.
- Skin cancer removal about five months ago. Healed without problems.

**Vitals:**
- Blood pressure elevated in clinic. ER records also show elevated blood pressure.

**Physical exam:**
- Neck: supple, no venous distention noted [verify: transcribed as "fibular venous distention"]
- Cardiac: regular rate and rhythm, no murmur
- Lungs: fine bilateral crackles
- Extremities: trace bilateral lower extremity edema

**Data reviewed:**
- ECG: stable. Shows left ventricular hypertrophy, which the physician attributed as the cause of his congestive heart failure.
- Echocardiogram: left ventricular pumping function slightly reduced, stable.
- Skin biopsy pathology: reviewed; all lesion appears removed and results are fine.

**Assessment:**
1. Shortness of breath in the ED, likely exacerbation of chronic congestive heart failure, with probable fluid retention related to dietary sodium intake.
2. Congestive heart failure with left ventricular hypertrophy; LV systolic function slightly reduced, stable on echo. Currently on appropriate medication therapy per physician.
3. Elevated blood pressure, in clinic and in ED. To be discussed further.
4. Status post cataract removal, no current vision problems.
5. Status post skin cancer removal, pathology reviewed, no concerns.

**Plan:**
1. Furosemide (Lasix) 80 mg by mouth once daily, ordered as an extra dose for fluid retention.
2. Carvedilol 25 mg by mouth twice daily, ordered.
3. Continue current heart failure medication therapy.
4. No medication changes needed for cataract surgery or skin cancer care.
5. Blood pressure to be discussed with patient [details not captured in transcript].
6. Nurse to see patient before discharge.

VISIT NOTE (draft)

Patient: George (last name not stated in transcript)
Visit type: Office visit
Clinician: Not named in transcript

**Chief complaint:** Numbness and tingling in the fingers and pain in the wrist/hand.

**History of present illness:**
- Right wrist and hand pain and numbness for approximately several months, per patient.
- Onset was gradual and spontaneous. Patient does not recall a specific cause.
- Symptoms occur mainly at night. Patient wakes with the hand asleep and has to shake it out.
- Numbness involves all fingers, more prominent in the thumb and index finger. Patient also reports occasional numbness in the little finger.
- Patient reports weakness in the left hand and drops objects because of difficulty feeling them.
- Patient reports no problems with the right hand. Patient's statements about laterality (right vs. left) are inconsistent in the transcript and should be verified.

**Occupational history:** Landscaping. Heavy labor with repetitive raking and digging, performed daily.

**Social history:** Alcohol use of one to two beers on Fridays and Saturdays.

**Past history:** No prior diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis reported by patient. No one has previously mentioned it to the patient.

**Physical exam:**
- Heart and lungs: Listened to, reported as normal ("that's good").
- Grip strength: Decreased on the left compared with the right.
- Sensation: Patient can feel touch on all fingers of the right hand. Sensation on the thumb side feels more altered than on the index finger side. Left-hand sensory findings were not separately described in the transcript.
- Tinel's sign: Positive bilaterally. Tapping over the wrists produces a tingling sensation in the fingertips on both sides.

**Assessment:** Clinician's impression is probable bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, likely related to repetitive occupational activity. Clinician noted that history and exam are consistent with this impression.

**Plan:**
1. Order EMG to assess electrical conduction in the fingers. Follow up on results.
2. Activity modification for approximately two weeks: avoid repetitive motions. Patient agreed to delegate repetitive tasks to other employees.
3. Wrist splint to be worn.
4. Ibuprofen 600 mg every six hours.
5. Return to clinic in two weeks to reassess. Consider further diagnostic testing or possible surgical release of nerve pressure if symptoms do not improve.

**Patient education and agreement:** Patient agreed with the plan ("sounds like a good first start").

**Disposition:** Discharged by nurse. Patient had no further questions.

**Items for clinician review:**
- Confirm symptomatic side(s). Patient described right-sided symptoms initially, then left-sided weakness and reported no right-hand problems.
- Left-hand sensory examination findings were not explicitly documented.

VISIT NOTE (draft)

**Patient:** Brittany
**Visit date:** Not stated in transcript

**Chief complaint:** Right foot pain

**HPI:**
Patient reports right foot pain after an injury while playing doubles tennis about a couple of days ago. She was volleying, got in front of another player, and fell on top of her right foot. She then twisted to catch herself and felt pain in the foot. She could not bear weight and had to be helped off the field. She has not been able to continue playing.

Treatment since injury: wrapped with ACE wrap, iced, kept elevated on a pillow, and took ibuprofen. Ibuprofen provides partial relief that wears off after a while.

Denies numbness. Reports she can still feel her foot.

**Past history:** Prior injury to the left foot (details not stated).

**Social history:** Right-handed. Plays tennis recreationally with friends; not currently taking lessons.

**Vitals:** BP 125/70, RR 18, Temp 97.1, SpO2 100%, Pulse approximately 60 bpm.

**Physical exam:**
- Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm. No murmur, rub, or gallop.
- Respiratory: A little bit of stridor noted. No wheezes or rales.
- Abdomen: No rebound or guarding.
- HEENT/Skin: Head symmetrical. Mucous membranes normal. Not hot to touch.
- Right foot:
  - Bruising of plantar and dorsal aspects.
  - Swelling at midfoot.
  - Tenderness to palpation of midfoot. (Patient answered no when asked whether palpation hurt.)
  - Positive piano key test, first and second metatarsals.
  - Warm to touch.
- Right foot neurovascular: Capillary refill less than 3 seconds. Dorsalis pedis pulse strong. Sensation intact to light touch.
- Left foot: Capillary refill appropriate. Pedal pulses strong. Sensation intact.

**Imaging:** X-ray right foot (reviewed by clinician): Subtle dorsal displacement of the base of the second metatarsal. 3 mm separation of the first and second metatarsal bases. Bony fragment in the Lisfranc joint space.

**Assessment:**
Right foot pain consistent with Lisfranc fracture involving the base of the second metatarsal.

**Plan:**
- Recommend surgery for right foot: plates and screws to place bones in proper position. Explained risk of poor bone alignment and ligament healing, which could lead to loss of arch (flat foot) and arthritis.
- Order MRI of right foot to further assess fracture and ligament injury.
- Surgery is planned as day surgery. Patient will need a driver to take her home. Right foot is her dominant foot and she is right-handed.
- Post-op: Clinic follow-up in about one week. Cast and crutches. Non-weight-bearing on right foot for 6 to 8 weeks, then gradual weight-bearing based on progress.
- Physical therapy after surgery to strengthen muscles and return to peak performance.
- Patient understands she will be out for the rest of the tennis season.
- Risks of surgery (including bleeding, loss of sensation, nerve damage) to be reviewed. Consent paperwork to be provided by MA. Patient encouraged to ask questions before and after the procedure.
